# The Code Behind the Figures {#sec-the-code}

Every figure and number in this book is computed when the book is built, by a small
Python package, `optimlab`, that implements each method from scratch with NumPy and
JAX. This appendix explains how that code is organized, how it is checked, and how to
run it. Nothing in the chapters depends on reading it.

## One interface for every method

Almost every method takes the same two things in and gives the same thing back. A
**problem** bundles an objective $f$, a starting point and, optionally, a search box and
known minima; gradients and Hessians are computed by automatic differentiation
(JAX) unless supplied by hand. A **result** reports the final point and value, the
number of iterations, whether the method's own stopping test was met, and the full
history of iterates, which is what the figures draw. Because of this shared shape, any
general-purpose method can run on any problem, which is what
[Choosing an Algorithm](appendix-choosing-an-algorithm.qmd) exploits. Methods for
special problem classes (linear programs, least squares, composite and constrained
problems) take their own problem types.

| part of the package | contents | used in |
|---|---|---|
| `core` | the problem and result types, automatic differentiation | all |
| `landscapes` | test functions (sphere, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin, Himmelblau, …) | @sec-geometry, @sec-derivative-free |
| `optimizers` | every iterative method in the book | @sec-gradient-methods to @sec-derivative-free |
| `linalg` | SVD, least squares, ridge, equality-constrained QP | @sec-geometry, @sec-least-squares, @sec-constraints |
| `inference` | MLE, MAP, Laplace, Metropolis–Hastings, EM | @sec-estimation |
| `highdim` | networks as problems, Lanczos, loss slices, mode connectivity, NTK | @sec-high-dim |
| `inverse`, `control`, `ml`, `problems` | the applications | @sec-applications |
| `viz` | every figure builder, sharing one colorblind-checked theme | all |
| `backends` | adapters to SciPy, CVXPY and Optuna, used as independent checks | @sec-linear-programming to @sec-derivative-free |

## How the code is checked

Each method has its own test file, and the tests check real behavior against known
answers rather than only that the code runs: convergence to known minima, agreement with
closed-form solutions, and agreement with independent solvers (SciPy's HiGHS for linear
programs, CVXPY for constrained problems, Optuna for black-box search). The
*Checked by* link at the end of each method section in the book points to its tests.

## Running it yourself

The source is on [GitHub]({{< var repo >}}). With [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/)
installed:

```bash
uv sync --extra viz --extra dev --extra docs   # install
uv run pytest                                  # run the tests
quarto render docs                             # build this book (needs Quarto)
```

### Interactive notebooks

Eight [marimo](https://marimo.io) notebooks let you change a problem or a setting and
watch the figures update, one per topic:

| notebook | explores | chapter |
|---|---|---|
| `gradient_descent_explorer.py` | step sizes, momentum and solver races on test landscapes | @sec-gradient-methods |
| `lp_polytope_explorer.py` | the simplex path on an editable linear program | @sec-linear-programming |
| `regularization_path_explorer.py` | ridge and lasso paths | @sec-least-squares |
| `central_path_explorer.py` | the barrier method's central path | @sec-constraints |
| `bayesian_posterior_explorer.py` | Laplace versus MCMC on a coin-flip posterior | @sec-estimation |
| `loss_landscape_explorer.py` | loss slices and Hessian spectra of small networks | @sec-high-dim |
| `control_explorer.py` | LQR cost weights and initial state, re-solved live | @sec-applications |
| `solver_arena_explorer.py` | every method on a chosen test function | @sec-choosing |

```bash
uv run marimo edit notebooks/marimo/gradient_descent_explorer.py
```

The notebooks need a local Python: the package uses JAX, which cannot run inside a web
browser, so they cannot be embedded in these pages.
